{{Short description|Type of simulation in vehicle dynamics}}
[[File:Magic Formula Curve.png|thumb|right|Example of the [[slip angle]] curve obtained from a Pacejka Magic Formula empirical tire model.]]

In [[vehicle dynamics]], a '''tire model''' is a type of [[multibody simulation]] used to simulate the behavior of [[tire]]s. In current vehicle simulator models, the tire model is the weakest and most difficult part to simulate.<ref>Rachel Evans ''[https://www.vi-grade.com/dynatc/attachments-0542-361e/Automotive%20Testing%20Technology%20oct2015.pdf Quantum leaps]'', Automotive Testing Technology International, September 2015, p.43 quote from [[MTS Systems Corporation|MTS]]' Mark Gillian: "''From an OEM perspective, thermal modelling may be overkill but the tire models are still the weak point of any vehicle model''"</ref><ref name="Nakajima2019">Yukio Nakajima (2019) ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=dQGQDwAAQBAJ Advanced Tire Mechanics]'', ch.11 pp.707-710</ref>

Tire models can be classified on their accuracy and complexity, in a spectrum that goes from more simple empirical models to more complex physical models that are theoretically grounded.<ref name="Monsma2015">Monsma, Saskia (2015) [https://research.aalto.fi/en/publications/feel-the-tire-tire-influence-on-drivers-handling-assessment/ Feel the Tire - Tire Influence on Driver’s Handling Assessmen], phd thesis at Aalto University, pp.19-20</ref> Empirical models include [[Hans B. Pacejka]]'s ''Magic Formula'', while physically based models include brush models (although they are still quite simplified), and more complex and detailed physical models include RMOD-K, FTire and Hankook.<ref>Pacejka (2012) ch.2</ref><ref name="Monsma2015"/> Theoretically-based models can be in turn classified from more approximate to more complex ones, going for example from the solid model, to the rigid ring model, to the flexural (elastic) ring model (like the Fiala model), and the most complex ones based on [[finite element method]]s.<ref name="Nakajima2019"/>

Brush models were very popular in the 1960s and '70s, after which Pacejka's models became widespread for many applications.<ref name="Conte2014">Francesco Conte (2014) [http://kth.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:805263/FULLTEXT01.pdf EXPANDING THE BRUSH TIRE MODEL FOR ENERGY STUDIES] (Thesis) p.10</ref>

==Classification by purpose==
===Driving dynamics models===
* Brush model (Dugoff, Fancher and Segel, 1970)<ref name="Monsma2015"/>
* Hohenheim tire model (physical approach [1])
* [[Hans B. Pacejka#Magic Formula tire models|Pacejka Magic Formula Tire]] (Bakker, Nyborg and Pacejka, 1987)<ref name="Monsma2015"/>
* TameTire (semi-physical approach)<ref name="Nakajima2019"/>
* TMeasy (semi-physical approach)
* Stretched string tire model (Fiala 1954)

===Comfort models===
* BRIT (Brush and Ring Tire)
* CDTire (Comfort and Durability Tire)
* Ctire (Comfort tire)
* Dtire (Dynamical Nonlinear Spatial Tire Model)
* FTire (Flexible Structure Tire Model)<ref name="Monsma2015"/>
* RMOD-K (Comfort and Durability Tire)<ref name="Monsma2015"/>
* SWIFT (Short Wavelength Intermediate Frequency Tire) (Besselink, Pacejka, Schmeitz, & Jansen, 2005)<ref name="Monsma2015"/><ref name="Nakajima2019"/>

==Applications==
Fully physics-based tire models have been typically too computational expensive to be run in realtime driving simulations. For example, to since CDTire/3D, a physics-based tire model, cannot be run in realtime, for realtime applications typically an equivalent semi-empirical "magic formula" type of model, called CDTire/Realtime, is derived from it through experiments and a [[Regression analysis|regression algorithm]].<ref>Calabrese, F., Bäcker, M., & Gallrein, A. (2020) ''Exploring simulator technology for tire development'', in Peter E. Pfeffer (Ed.) ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=zZO7DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA772 10th International Munich Chassis Symposium 2019: chassis.tech plus]'', p.772</ref>

In 2016, a slightly less accurate version of FTire, a physics-based tire model, was adapted to be run in real time.<ref>[https://www.cosin.eu/wp-content/uploads/FTire_Artikel_VehicleDynamic_1601213.pdf FTire and ASM – Sophisticated Models for Real-Time Vehicle Dynamics Simulation], [[dSPACE GmbH]], 2016</ref> This realtime version of FTire was shown in 2018 to run on a 2,7&nbsp;GHz 12 Core Intel Xeon E5 (2014, 22&nbsp;nm process, about $2000), with 900 contact road/[[contact patch]] elements, a sample frequency of 4.0&nbsp;kHz including thermal and wear simulation.<ref name="Gipser2018">Gipser, Michael and  Baumann, Mario (2018) ''[https://www.cosin.eu/wp-content/uploads/VI-grade_2018.pdf FTire on the Driving Simulator]'', pp.13-17, Presentation at International VI-Grade Users Conference, Milano, May 8–9, 2018</ref>

The typical tire model sampling rate used in automotive simulators is 1&nbsp;kHz.<ref name="Teodosio2021">Teodosio, L., Alferi, G., Genovese, A., Farroni, F., Mele, B., Timpone, F., & Sakhnevych, A. (2021) ''[https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11012-021-01310-w A numerical methodology for thermo-fluid dynamic modelling of tyre inner chamber: towards real time applications]'', Meccanica, 56(3), 549-567.</ref> However, running at higher frequencies, like 2&nbsp;kHz, might mitigate lowered numerical stability in some scenarios, and might increase the model accuracy in frequency domain above 
about 250&nbsp;Hz.<ref name="Gipser2018"/>
